articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Lower, Treasury Yields Hit Fresh 24-Year Highs — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens Lower, Treasury Yields Hit Fresh 24-Year Highs — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The yields on key U.S. Treasury bonds touched fresh 24-year highs Wednesday, as the latest global bond sell-off picked up steam.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose as high as 5.36% and the 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.73% — the highest levels for each since 2002.
Benchmark government bonds in France and Italy also rose sharply. The yield on the U.K. 30-year government bond hit its highest level since 1998.
When bonds fall, their yields rise.
U.S. bond yields pulled back later in the day, following a Treasury Department auction of $39 billion worth of 10-year bonds, for which there was strong demand.
But at 5.3%, the yield on the auctioned bonds was the highest of any U.S. government sale of 10-year debt since November 2000.
“Bottom line, for whatever reason, likely the 24 yr highs in rates, brought out the buyers and resulted in a great auction,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners. “In response, the 10 yr yield has backed off to 5.27% from 5.31% just prior to the results.”
The bond rout had sent stocks tumbling early in the day, but as the decades-high yields eased, so did losses among the major stock indexes.
After notching record highs on Tuesday, both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq ended the day down about 0.2%. The Dow fell 341 points or 0.6%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium sized companies, declined 1.3%.
European stock markets had seen steeper selling. The Stoxx 600 index ended lower by 1%, while benchmark indexes in France and Germany closed down by around 1.3%. Italy’s FTSE MIB index slid 2.5%.
As stocks fell, oil prices flipped between gains and losses, but largely hovered around their highly-elevated levels. Brent crude oil declined 0.5% but was still at more than $100 per barrel in afternoon trading.
The recent rise in bond yields only compounds the pain for governments around the world that have seen their borrowing costs soar since the start of the year.
Overnight, International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva warned that governments urgently need to take steps to get their unprecedented debt under control.
She also predicted that government bond yields around the world would remain under pressure because of the ever-expanding artificial intelligence boom.
“Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years, as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates,” Georgieva said in a speech. “Higher interest rates now put an end to that.”
Her comments followed multiple reports that Elon Musk’s SpaceX is planning to raise $40 billion in cash to buy AI chips from Nvidia. NBC News has not independently confirmed the reports and SpaceX did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
But if the company follows through, that borrowed $40 billion would join hundreds of billions more in bond sales by AI-linked companies in recent years. The companies are using the money to build data centers and buy equipment with which to fill them.
Some economists believe that the vast sums of money being borrowed by private AI companies could pile additional pressure on government bond yields.
“France may be on the verge of a full-blown debt crisis,” wrote Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research on Sunday.
He noted that the yield on French 10-year government bonds has risen the most of any major economy this year. Coming in second  is the United States, while Italy, a country traditionally viewed as far more risky by the bond markets, comes in third.
Apollo economic strategist Huw van Steenis wrote in a Wednesday note, “Hyperscalers have raised $48 billion in bonds in European currencies this year, which is already more than triple the entire amount of 2025.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Levi Strauss hikes profit guidance after tariff refunds, but its sales outlook is less optimistic
articles.title_zh: Levi Strauss hikes profit guidance after tariff refunds, but its sales outlook is less optimistic
articles.content_orig:
Levi Strauss on Wednesday increased its profit outlook after it received tariff refunds, but gave less rosy revenue guidance.
The denim retailer raised its adjusted earnings per share expectation for the full fiscal year to between $1.54 and $1.56, from a previous range of $1.46 to $1.52. Analysts were expecting a range of between $1.52 and $1.59, according to LSEG.
The company also lowered its net revenue growth guidance for the full year to 7%, the bottom of its previously provided range of a 7% to 7.5% increase.
Shares of Levi were roughly flat in extended trading after initially rising.
For its fiscal third quarter, the denim retailer said it saw a 4% increase in net revenues in the Americas, though revenue in the U.S. decreased 1%. It also reported an operating margin of 13.8% for the quarter, compared to 10.8% in the same quarter last year, boosted by tariff refunds that contributed 4.9% to operating margin and gross margin.
Levi also said its tariff refunds contributed a 16-cent benefit to its earnings per share, of which 5 cents were "redeployed to support the business." On a call with analysts, CEO Michelle Gass said that money is going toward marketing and promotions during the holiday season.
Here's how Levi performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the three-month period ending Aug. 30, Levi reported net income of $168.6 million, or 43 cents per share, down from $218.1 million, or 55 cents per share, the year prior.
Sales rose roughly 4% to $1.61 billion from $1.54 billion last year.
Levi said direct-to-consumer net revenues increased 2% in the quarter, but comparable sales were roughly flat. DTC comprised 45% of total net revenue in the third quarter, the company said. On the other hand, wholesale revenues increased 6% for the quarter.
"While we delivered strong results across much of the business, our DTC performance fell short of our expectations during the quarter," Gass said on the call with analysts. "We have a clear understanding of what worked and what did not, and we have already taken targeted actions to improve performance."
The company previously said it's been seeing broad-based growth across its business segments, including its core Levi's and its premium blue tab.
Last month, the company announced John Vandemore will take over as chief financial officer effective Nov. 1, succeeding Harmit Singh, who announced his retirement in April.

Webull ( BULL ) stock plunged 19% on Wednesday after US lawmakers reportedly flagged that the company is "tied in structural ways" to China's government, risking its regulatory standing in the US.
The stock faced its worst daily drop since April 17, 2025, according to Dow Jones and FactSet market data. Over the past month, the stock has cratered by 40%.
On Wednesday, CNBC reported that a bipartisan House Select Committee on China assessment found that the company poses a national security risk and that concerns about its operations have "escalated" over the past year.
Webull is a digital investment platform headquartered in St. Petersburg, Fla. Yet the congressional report stated there was "a profound gap" between how the company marketed itself as a US company and how it is actually controlled.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the report said, per CNBC.
The company was founded in 2016 by former Alibaba ( BABA ) employee Anquan Wang and was affiliated with the Chinese holding company Hunan Fumi Information Technology. It went public on the Nasdaq via a special-purpose acquisition merger with SK Growth Opportunities in 2025.
Webull has 28.2 million users, and roughly 85% of its funded accounts are held by US users, according to SEC filings. The committee raised concerns that Webull's US customer data could be exposed should Webull be compelled to comply with Chinese laws and government requests.
Webull pushed back on the report, telling CNBC that it contained "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions."

articles.title_zh: Christa Pike’s attorneys believed she was brain-dead before she woke up ‘to the shock of everyone’
articles.content_orig:
A judge sided with the Tennessee inmate and ruled that evidence from her botched execution should be preserved.
• Christa Pike’s attorneys said they believed she was “brain-dead” after her botched execution last week – before she woke up and started talking. She is “ angry and confused about everything right now,” but is “very aware that the state tried to execute her,” attorney Randy Spivey told reporters. Pike has a “long road to recovery,” he added.
• The attorneys spoke after they were granted an emergency motion ordering the state to preserve evidence related to the execution. This includes 911 calls and communications between any state officials as well as physical evidence, Judge I’Ashea Myles said.
• Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Our live coverage has ended. Scroll down for updates on today’s court hearing and the latest from Christa Pike’s attorneys following her botched execution.
A judge ruled today the state of Tennessee must preserve all evidence related to Christa Pike’s failed execution.
This includes 911 calls and communications between any state officials as well as physical evidence, Judge I’Ashea Myles said, after hearing arguments.
Pike is conscious and speaking, her attorneys said, despite it appearing the night before that she was brain-dead and would be taken off life support. She was hospitalized after surviving two ostensibly lethal doses of pentobarbital last week.
Lauren del Valle, Maureen Chowdhury, August Phillips and Rebekah Riess contributed reporting.
Lawyers for a Texas man are asking a judge to pause his execution , citing the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
Jamaal Howard is set to be executed by lethal injection later today , the first since Pike. Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery.
In the filing, the attorneys requested more information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use, the AP reported.
Pike’s lawyers allege that issues with IV lines allowed the barbiturate to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream .
There is another execution scheduled in Florida next week, a state that has carried out the most executions so far this year, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . All of them used lethal injection, data shows.
Michelle Nowell, a Tennessee resident, said the state has “paid enough” for Christa Pike, citing the state’s rising bill from the continuation of her case after her botched execution last week.
“We have paid for Christa Pike, and now we’re paying for attorneys, and now we’re paying for hospital bills, and now they’re talking about lawsuits,” Nowell told CNN. “And the worst part is that Colleen has been forgotten.”
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a job training facility.
Nowell pushed back on Pike’s attorneys statement describing her botched execution as “cruel and unusual” and to those who say Pike has “changed” in her more than 30 years in prison.
“Colleen is the one that knew cruel and unusual punishment,” she said.
Nowell said the state handled Pike’s execution “absolutely terribly.”
“I think it’s shameful,” Nowell said. “I’m a Tennessean, born and raised, a voter, and I know that our governor is going to be leaving soon, in January, and my hope is that Gov. (Bill) Lee will do the right thing and follow through with this execution.”
Jerri Green, Tennessee’s Democratic candidate for governor, who is running against Republican US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, has vowed to “enact a moratorium on all future executions,” in the state.
“True respect for the victims and their families means a justice system built on honesty, fairness, and safety, not cruelty, endless systemic failure, and secrecy. The facts are clear: the death penalty has proven to be an ineffective deterrent to violent crime, it is vastly more expensive than life imprisonment, and it is riddled with bias,” her statement reads in part.
“While the rest of the world reels from a botched execution that went horribly wrong, Blackburn is doubling down, calling to bring back the electric chair. That is barbaric, and it has no place in our state,” Green said of her opponent.
“As a public defender who has seen the devastating flaws in our justice system firsthand, my stance remains unshakeable: true pro-life values mean rejecting the death penalty entirely, and as Governor, I will enact a moratorium on all future executions,” she added.
Christa Pike’s attorney requested that her hand be unshackled as she receives medical care at a hospital after her botched execution.
Myles asked Ihnen had an affidavit from the medical personnel stating this request, and the attorney said he didn’t, but could provide it. The judge said she would make a decision after the document is submitted.
The state interjected on the request and pointed to Pike’s “escape history.” The judge said the request only includes unshackling Pike’s hand, not feet, and that she is reserving her judgment on this matter until she hears from the medical personnel.
Christa Pike’s attorney said he noticed “extraordinary” swelling of her hands following her botched execution attempt.
“Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” he said. “The swelling was extraordinary, and that’s, that’s probably as far as I can go.”
Earlier, in court, her attorneys requested that Pike’s hand be unshackled while she is in the hospital due to the “extensive damage done to her arms and hands.”
Attorneys for Christa Pike thought she was brain-dead Monday and would be taken off life support the following day, but “to the shock of everyone,” on Tuesday, she woke up and began to talk, attorney Randy Spivey with the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender said.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” Spivey said.
Pike has pneumonia and a blood clot in one of her arms, and she is not able to swallow yet and is therefore not eating, according to Spivey.
“She cannot move either of her arms. Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms. But we do know that there’s a long road ahead,” he added.
The botched execution of Christa Pike was “foreseeable and foreseen,” one of her lawyers, Randy Spivey, reiterated today after a court hearing to preserve evidence after the incident.
“What happened to Christa is exactly what the state was warned would happen, and there are so many questions that need to be answered, not by Christa — but by the state of Tennessee,” he said at a news conference outside the courthouse.
Her lawyer said Pike was “at peace” in the moments before her execution. She was “kind and polite” as officials struggled to set the IV lines for more than an hour, Spivey said.
“And then she woke up in a hospital surrounded by people she didn’t know with a tube down her throat. We don’t know the toll all of this will take, but Christa is a survivor, and we remain hopeful,” Spivey said.
Pike’s attorneys previously said they had warned courts beforehand that Pike’s vein issues would make it difficult to carry out the lethal injection.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.
An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said.
The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said.
Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter.
CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores.
Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York.
Flores is expected to appear at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer will ask that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial.
More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns.
Several of the Americans have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained.
The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. Tomeu Vadell , Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned.
All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report.
That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.”
This story is developing and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.title_zh: Lawmakers probe St. Pete stock trading firm’s Chinese ties
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

articles.title_zh: World Wide Technology Raceway Celebrates Historic Success of 15th Annual NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals
articles.content_orig:
Last Updated on October 7, 2026 by WWTR
Nearly 3.5 million television viewers make the event the second biggest broadcast in NHRA history.
MADISON, Ill. (Oct. 7, 2026) – World Wide Technology Raceway is celebrating a historic and highly successful NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals weekend that delivered a sold-out crowd, record-setting performances on the racetrack, and one of the largest television audiences in NHRA history, further elevating the visibility of the St. Louis and Metro East region on a national stage.
FOX’s Sunday coverage of the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals averaged 1.896 million viewers, making it the second-most viewed NHRA telecast in NHRA history. The broadcast also reached a peak audience of 3.247 million viewers, showcasing the excitement of NHRA Drag Racing to millions of viewers across the country and around the world.
The milestone television audience followed a Saturday sellout at World Wide Technology Raceway, marking NHRA’s 11th sellout event date of the season during the sanctioning body’s landmark 75th Anniversary season.
Fans attending the event witnessed an unforgettable weekend featuring new track records, a world-record Pro Mod performance, championship implications across multiple categories, and the electric atmosphere that has made the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals one of the premier stops on the NHRA Mission Foods Drag Racing Series schedule.
Beyond the competition, the event once again demonstrated its importance as one of the Midwest’s leading tourism and economic development drivers. Thousands of visitors traveled to the St. Louis metropolitan area for the event, filling hotels, restaurants, attractions, and businesses throughout both Missouri and Illinois while generating significant economic activity on both sides of the Mississippi River.
“This was an extraordinary weekend for NHRA, for World Wide Technology Raceway, and for the entire St. Louis region,” said Curtis Francois, Owner and CEO of World Wide Technology Raceway. “A sellout crowd on Saturday and one of the largest television audiences in NHRA history on Sunday reflects the passion of our fans and the tremendous momentum behind the sport. Just as importantly, this event served as a powerful showcase for St. Louis and the Metro East, introducing millions of viewers to our region and reinforcing why major motorsports events are such important tourism and economic engines for our communities.”
Francois added, “The NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals generates benefits well beyond the raceway gates. Visitors stay in our hotels, dine in our restaurants, shop in local stores, and enjoy attractions throughout both Illinois and Missouri. The impact is regional, and we are proud to host an event that contributes meaningfully to the economy while creating unforgettable memories for fans from across North America.”
The record audience and strong attendance continue a trend of growth for both the NHRA and World Wide Technology Raceway, which has become one of the sport’s marquee destinations. The success of the event further highlights the strength of the partnership between NHRA, FOX Sports, local tourism organizations, community stakeholders, and the thousands of dedicated fans who make the NAPA Auto Parts NHRA Midwest Nationals a cornerstone event on the motorsports calendar.

articles.title_orig: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.title_zh: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.content_orig:
Pennsylvania’s explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it’s the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania’s health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April , when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths— a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, measles outbreaks and cases have come roaring back in the past few years. A large outbreak in Texas that spanned January­–August 2025 ended with 762 cases , while an outbreak in South Carolina ended in April with 997 cases , the previous record holder. Pennsylvania exceeds that handily with its 1,066 outbreak-linked cases as of today. With 34 new infections reported since Monday, the outbreak does not appear to be close to ending.
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Elimination is earned and maintained with vaccination rates that prevent continuous transmission of the virus during a 12-month period. In November, experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—which acts as a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data on whether the US has lost its measles elimination status. Experts widely expect the US has lost the status. Canada lost its elimination status in 2025.
The last measles outbreak that was larger than the current one in Pennsylvania was an outbreak in New York, which spanned 1990–1991 and infected more than 4,500 in all.
Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency over rising measles cases there. There have been at least 108 cases in the state. The emergency declaration expands the pool of healthcare workers who can provide measles vaccinations, newly including paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists, and midwives. It also allows nurses, in addition to physicians, to order measles tests.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement. “That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 3,887 measles cases nationwide for the year. That is the highest tally in the US since 1991, when there were 9,643 cases. Experts are becoming yet more anxious as measles outbreaks stretch into the fall; in the pre-vaccine era, measles was typically a virus of the late winter and early spring . Experts are concerned that spread could accelerate further in favorable conditions.

articles.title_orig: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
articles.title_zh: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
articles.content_orig:
Researchers say a small fossil from the middle Jurassic provides some of the oldest evidence of chewing and swallowing as well as suckling — all distinctly mammalian traits. Chang-Fu Zhou/Shandong University of Science and Technology hide caption
Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.
"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo , a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.
It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.
This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature , was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.
Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.
"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.
The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.
"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."
One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.
The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.
An artistic rendering of Megacauda sungei . The animal was the size of a chihuahua and a bit of a mutt. Its back end resembled a platypus but its sharp teeth suggested it was a predator. April Neander/University of Chicago hide caption
These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.
"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.
There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.
The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.
The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.
With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.
This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.
The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."
Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.
Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.
"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."
This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.
"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor , a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."
Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.
"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."
For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.
"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."
By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

articles.title_orig: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.title_zh: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.content_orig:
Take a closer look at the "Make AI Work for Americans Act," and learn why it's important to help workers and families navigate AI disruption.
While there’s no consensus on exactly how artificial intelligence will affect workers, it’s clear that the technology will change who works and how they work. On September 24, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly introduced a bill called the Make AI Work for Americans Act . It prioritizes helping workers and families navigate the disruption that AI will cause through a federal trust fund paid for by the large AI companies set to profit most from AI’s boom.
In the past three years, the cumulative value of AI-linked firms has increased by $27 trillion across the value of the entire U.S. stock market; this accounts for 36% of value. There have been persistent concerns about whether this enormous spending—including on physical infrastructure and software development—is part of a bubble . Right now, this  technology is important to economic growth, as AI spending accounted for 40% of U.S. economic growth in the past year.
There are growing concerns about what the growth of AI means for American workers. OpenAI predicted that in the short term, 18% of jobs were at risk of automation, and 24% may see declining employment as the composition of tasks within occupations shifts.
Some estimates have found that of the highly AI-exposed workers, about 70% may be able to adapt fairly easily. But adaptation will likely be harder for over 6 million workers who are primarily employed in clerical and administrative roles.
What we can say now is that it’s likely that the effects of AI on workers will be concentrated in certain occupations. Last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released AI exposure categories organized by occupation that track how well the capabilities of AI match job tasks, and over 200 occupations are facing very high exposure , such as customer service representatives and web developers. The billion (trillion?) dollar question is whether occupations that are highly exposed will be able to adapt .
It’s also clear that people are worried about how AI is going to impact their jobs. A 2026 poll on AI found that 7 in 10 Americans think that AI will cut jobs. Polling from Groundwork Collaborative and Ipsos found that only 6% of respondents believe that the benefits of AI will mostly or all go to workers, and two-third of workers say that AI will make work harder, not easier.
Workers are doing their best to keep up, and a March 2026 national survey found that to compete with AI tools or avoid potential layoffs, 81% of workers are changing their behavior at work.
In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, universities are focused on developing technologies for physical AI , and the city is now home to 100 AI and robotics organizations. At the same time, Pittsburgh residents have pushed back against data centers due to their impact on the environment, pollution, and energy costs. Allegheny County is considering prohibiting data center development on county-owned land, and Pennsylvania has slowed data center development statewide.
In Iowa, rural communities like Salix are pushing back against data center projects; eight counties in the state already have moratoriums on data center development. Across the country, rural counties account for about two-thirds of planned data center projects, but they tend to see fewer benefits from these investments compared to cities. When a data center opens in a county, employment rises on average by about 3.5% and wages by 5%, but the gains from investment are experienced far more in urban counties than rural ones.
A third of South Carolinians believe that their employers will not protect them from having their jobs replaced by AI. At the same time, companies like Google are investing billions in the state’s cloud and AI infrastructure, i.e. data centers : Google’s 2025 investment is one of the largest technology investments in state history at $9 billion dollars .
Legislation like the Make AI Work for Americans Act is an important step and crucial part of supporting workers and their communities through this AI disruption. Importantly, it asks the companies profiting most from this technology to invest in the workers facing changing labor opportunities.
Heather Boushey is a professor of practice at the Kleinman Center. Boushey served in the Biden administration as a member of the Council of Economic Advisers and chief economist to the President’s Investing in America cabinet.

articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday has ‘borne fruit in my own life,’ says Pope Leo
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday has ‘borne fruit in my own life,’ says Pope Leo
articles.content_orig:
The aim of World Mission Sunday (Oct. 18), established 100 years ago by Pope Pius XI, has “borne fruit in my own life,” said Pope Leo XIV.
The pope reflected on the annual observance in a video message posted by Vatican News to its YouTube channel Oct. 7. A transcript of the message was also published on the Vatican’s website.
In January, Pope Leo XIV announced he had chosen the theme “One in Christ, united in mission” for this year’s celebration, with his message for the day encouraging “the whole Church to continue its missionary journey with joy and zeal in the Holy Spirit.”
Established by Pope Pius XI in 1926 and universally observed by 1927, World Mission Sunday is a dedicated day of “prayer and missionary promotion throughout the Catholic world,” according to its founding decree.
Held on the next-to-last Sunday of October, the observance also includes a collection that serves as the primary financial support for the Pontifical Mission Societies, a worldwide network operating at the service of the pope and consisting of four organizations designated as pontifical by Pope Pius XI in 1922.
The Society for the Propagation of the Faith supports the evangelization efforts of the local church; the Missionary Childhood Association educates children about their part in the church’s missionary outreach; the Society of St. Peter the Apostle trains the next generation of missionary clergy and consecrated religious; and the Pontifical Missionary Union focuses on forming clergy, religious and pastoral leaders more deeply in their role as evangelizers.
In his video message, Pope Leo said, “Looking back on my youth, I can see how the prayers offered to the Lord of the harvest mysteriously helped prepare my heart to hear Jesus’ call to follow him as an Augustinian missionary.”
The future pope served for years in Peru, a country particularly blessed by missionary priests, said Father Anthony D. Andreassi , a priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri in Brooklyn, New York, and a researcher for the Pontifical Mission Societies USA.
In an Oct. 5 interview with OSV News, Father Andreassi explained how the 20th century saw an uptick in the number of North American priests, both diocesan and religious, assigned to Latin America, where the Church already had a 500-year presence, but “never enough of a native clergy.”
The Augustinian Order “started sending people into Peru in the 1960s,” said Father Andreassi. “And then, all of a sudden, you see Robert Prevost” — who would eventually become Pope Leo XIV — “there in the 1980s.”
In his video message, Pope Leo said “the prayers and contributions of the faithful encouraged and sustained my missionary work in Peru, as well as that of countless others throughout the world.”
“For this reason, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who has supported World Mission Sunday over the years,” he added.
The pope said this year’s theme “invites us to reflect on the fundamental task of nurturing the Church’s unity in following Christ, particularly in our commitment and responsibility to spread the Gospel message of salvation to all people.”
Baptism makes each of the faithful “a member of the Body of Christ” with “a unique role in contributing to Jesus’ saving work.”
“Our Lord calls us to cooperate as one family, with the help of the Holy Spirit, to bring everyone everywhere into a communion of faith in Christ,” said Pope Leo.
He reaffirmed his appeal from his previously released message for the day, urging all to “commit to contributing to the great mission of evangelization — which is always a work of love — according to our own vocation and the gifts we have received.”
Prayers and “practical support” will be “a great help in bringing the Gospel of God’s love to everyone, especially the poorest and those most in need,” said the pope, quoting from his earlier message.
He thanked those who “carry on the legacy of World Mission Sunday” and “support generously the evangelizing mission of the Church throughout the world.”
Gina Christian is a multimedia reporter for OSV News. Follow her on X @GinaJesseReina.

To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes. Andreou told the AI agent that he got an email from his accountant and asked Autopilot to get her what she needs. Autopilot then used Hybrid Intelligence to search across different folders to find the documents, rename the files, zip them into a folder, and draft an email to send to the accountant with the zip file attached.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.
Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text. The new experience will be available starting this fall on Windows 11 PCs, according to Windows and Surface boss Pavan Davuluri.

articles.title_orig: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.title_zh: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.content_orig:
Imagine you’re a hotshot young New York gallerist whose rapidly rising artist has been invited to show in a group exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). But between this fall’s booths at Frieze London and Art Basel Paris, a detour to Venice, and micromanaging your unpaid interns, you can only go for a day. So, tragically, there’s no time to fit in your regular visit to Erewhon, for which there’s simply no New York equivalent, especially because the $36,000 initiation fee for the Kith Ivy padel club that houses the city’s only Erewhon tonic bar is prohibitive in this art market.
Well, I have good news for the few who can relate to these circumstances: LACMA announced this week that the Erewhon pop-up in its new David Geffen Galleries will now serve as the museum’s permanent cafe. Housed in a glass box beneath Peter Zumthor’s sprawling $720 million “ designed to disorient ” structure, the Erewhon cafe faces out toward Alexander Calder’s recently restored fountain, “ Three Quintains (Hello Girls) ” (1964).
Calder’s tripartite mobile is also the inspiration for a new (and pre-distressed) capsule apparel collection and a signature LACMA smoothie, made from organic mango, mandarin, pineapple, strawberry, and lion’s mane. The beverage's unnatural gray hue resembles the concrete of Zumthor’s design — only floating with blobs of Calderesque colors.
“This integration represents the perfect synergy between two brands inextricably rooted in Los Angeles culture,” Elizabeth Wiatt, senior vice president of strategic partnerships at LACMA, said in a press statement.
Much like the well-intentioned art world, whose ecosystem becomes more optimized but also more expensive and materialistic with each day, Erewhon is a far cry from the Taoist principles that guided its founders, Aveline and Michio Kushi, who established the first location in Boston in 1966. Today, the health-conscious “ premium ” grocery chain has become synonymous with a particular status-centric idea of LA, offering adaptogenic cocktails, celebrity-collaboration smoothies, and absurd oddities like a $12 cup of “ Sacred Water .”
For a museum that recently hosted the star-studded unveiling of Ed Ruscha's poster for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new film Digger (2026), the Erewhon partnership is fitting. After all, it holds up a mirror to today's world, wherein overpaying for a smoothie somehow makes it more delectable, and institutional and commercial industry partnerships made under the guise of "community" are normalized.
Look no further than Erewhon President Josephine Antoci's euphemistic statement about the new LACMA cafe: “It’s a place for all to gather and make memories for years to come.”

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.
Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms . She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.
The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology” . They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.
At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.
On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”
Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”
The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.
In an interview with local media , Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.
She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.
Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”
The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.
On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.
According to the Baikal Medical Journal , health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.
“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.
“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”

Microsoft ( MSFT ) unveiled its Nvidia ( NVDA )-powered Surface Laptop Ultra during an event in San Francisco, Calif., on Wednesday.
Designed to compete with Apple's ( AAPL ) MacBook Pro laptops for AI, video workloads, and gaming, the $2,599 Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most powerful Surface to date, thanks to its Arm ( ARM )-based Nvidia RTX Spark processor.
Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices, Pavan Davuluri, said the chip features up to a staggering 128GB of unified memory, giving it the ability to run demanding AI models that other laptops can't.
According to Tom Mainelli, IDC's group vice president of device and consumer research, the Surface Laptop Ultra will likely appeal to early adopters across both the consumer and enterprise spaces.
"Ultimately, the cost is a big driver," Mainelli told Yahoo Finance. "But you're also going to get to a point where you want to make decisions about what data goes to the cloud, what data stays locally, and then you will be thinking about the orchestration layers."
Orchestration is the process of determining which AI models and agents to use, when, and for what purpose. For instance, you wouldn't want to use an expensive cloud-based model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to perform a task that a free, local model installed on your PC can handle.
During Wednesday's event, Microsoft executive vice president of Windows and devices explained that the company is bringing hybrid AI capabilities and AI agent security to Windows via a series of updates.
The enterprise and consumer tech industries have been leaning heavily into local AI models as an alternative to cloud-based models and agents. Kicking off a new arms race in the laptop and desktop space.
Read more: Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft are keeping the stock market afloat
Microsoft demonstrated the Surface Laptop Ultra's performance in a video clip showing it running the video game "Gears of War: E Day," GitHub Copilot, and the video editing platform DaVinci Resolve at the same time, something that would chew up a standard laptop.
When it comes to AI specifically, Microsoft says the Surface Laptop Ultra offers 4.3x faster AI image generation than a MacBook Pro with Apple's M5 Pro chip and 6.2x faster video generation.
The PC industry, like the rest of the tech sector, is contending with the ongoing shortage of memory and storage chips. That's forced companies to raise the prices of their devices, cutting into overall sales.
But, so far, those increased prices have helped insulate device makers from the worst of the sales declines.

articles.title_orig: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.title_zh: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.content_orig:
Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.
Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".
"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.
While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".
Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.
But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."
Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".
That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".
"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."
Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.
Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.
Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

articles.title_orig: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.title_zh: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.content_orig:
A pie safe, a sausage rope, and a model of the universe are among the curious objects in Peasant’s Burlesque, curated by Stace Brandt.
Quick Bit by Monica Lynn Manoski
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
It was a subtly crisp afternoon with soft light casting long shadows on the curving roads of North Andover as I drove with the windows down to my destination, Piep Haus Projects (PHP), a new experimental pop-up art space hosted at the home of artist Leah Piepgras. I followed a series of hand-painted arrows up the driveway to the far end of a previously shag-carpeted house with the unmistakable vibes of a swingers pad, now transformed into a living space, artist studio, and exhibition room. On my way in, a young person with flowing dark hair snaked past me, weaving in and out of sculptures, down through the yard to the edge of Lake Cochichewick and back through to where I stood.
PHP’s inaugural show features works by Arthur Henderson, a MassArt graduate who now lives and works in “relative isolation” (other than the company of his wife and son) in the woods of Western Connecticut. “Peasant’s Burlesque ,” curated by Stace Brandt, brings together seventeen larger works—all completed since the start of the year—including fourteen sculptures, two woodblock prints, and a Portrait of the Artist at Work in ink on paper, with twenty-two small-scale sculptures housed separately in a cabinet.
Arthur Henderson, Big Red (front), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth with variable objects inside. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
A six-foot-wide wooden chandelier with snuffed candles drew me into the exhibition room in the far end of the house. Titled Model of the Universe from the outside looking in , it’s suspended from the vaulted ceiling with a charcoal-colored chain. The work’s seven distinct arms invite your eyes to return again and again to trace the irregular edges, which, although cut from plywood, have a hand-drawn quality.
​ Big Red (2026), a chestnut-colored pie cabinet with doors splayed, holds a curious accumulation of hand-carved items including a pipe, medicine cup, and a stack of Porterhouse steaks. Its plywood back bears chiseled hands spelling P-I-E-S-A-F-E in American Sign Language. Underneath its four legs, an ebony trap door gives a sense of dark mystery. I found myself imagining who or what is beneath it.
​A glowing ember box serves as a pedestal for a hand-hewn baguette and beer can. Custom-crafted box crates elevate other lovingly shaped objects, including Milkcrib , a four-walled resting place for an imagined gallon of milk, and Decoy (Skull in Repose) , a small sculpture resembling a bruised and tilted three-dimensional heart. Throughout the room things are placed casually—like how you might find a space left if someone weren’t expecting company. On my way out, I passed a staircase guarded by a string of sausage links and a sign marked “Champagne Room,” which made me smile and want to stay and snoop around.
(left) Detail view of objects inside Big Red including Steaks , 2026. (right) Big Red (back), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
The show exudes a whimsical, masculine energy, with each object serving as a breadcrumb to a larger narrative series the artist calls The Feast of the Butcher King . The objects in “Peasant’s Burlesque” are made from the perspective of the townsfolk who fall victim to the Butcher King in a retake on the folktale “Stone Soup.” The viewer enters a “set” where objects are contrived as offerings in exchange for the magic soup stone.
Brandt thoughtfully responded to the challenge of bringing Henderson’s purposely rough-hewn objects together with the newly renovated white cork-floored, multi-windowed project space. Henderson said, “What could’ve created a tension or competition instead feels very harmonious—a true conversation between the objects and their surroundings.”
​Arthur Henderson and Stace Brandt will be present with the work on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m. Between now and then, the space is open by appointment. Reach out to leah.piepgras@gmail.com for availability.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
articles.content_orig:
FlyDubai faces renewed scrutiny over its pilot screening after an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked his captain with an ax on an Israel-bound flight, raising questions about whether the airline's rapid expansion outpaced its ability to vet recruits.
The Sept. 30 attack aboard Flight FZ1073 sent the Boeing 737 MAX into a steep descent with 182 people aboard. Passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and another pilot traveling on the aircraft landed it in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, has classified the incident as a terrorist attack. Investigators continue examining physical and digital evidence, the suspect's motives, and any related links. Authorities have not announced final investigative findings.
Hamam al-Hammami, 29, joined FlyDubai in February. Oman Air previously barred him from flying over concerns about extremist views and reassigned him to administrative work, The Associated Press reported, citing officials and people familiar with the matter.
Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, confirmed that he completed three months of theoretical training in 2025 but was not selected for employment. The training was part of its application process, ABC News reported .
The Wall Street Journal reported that FlyDubai conducted a criminal background check before hiring him but did not contact Oman to vet his experience, citing a person familiar with the process.
In a separate report Wednesday , the Journal said that al-Hammami told investigators he sought airlines and routes that would take him to Israel and nearly carried out an attack during the summer before reconsidering, according to people briefed on the inquiry.
New Zealand police said Tuesday that he completed part of his flight training there between November 2018 and May 2019 for a British company. Australian counterterrorism authorities are also examining his ties to that country, Reuters reported .
Saudi authorities detained al-Hammami after the emergency landing and transferred him to the United Arab Emirates last Thursday. The airline and Emirati authorities have not publicly identified him, Reuters reported, while investigators in several countries continue reviewing his travel and training history.
FlyDubai says it is cooperating with investigators and coordinating with government authorities and regulators.
"The safety and wellbeing of our passengers, crew and operations remain our highest priority," the airline said in a statement .
Flights to and from Israel remain suspended while the investigation continues. The carrier says it will review the suspension as additional information becomes available and help passengers find alternative travel arrangements.
The scrutiny comes after years of growth. FlyDubai's workforce expanded from 3,682 employees at the end of 2021 to 6,763 at the end of 2025, according to company financial reports .
The airline carried a record 15.7 million passengers in 2025 and earned $531 million after tax. Its network reached 140 destinations in 58 countries, while its fleet grew to 97 aircraft.
The carrier serves destinations including Kabul and Damascus, providing links to places many Western airlines avoid.
"FlyDubai continued the whole time, they didn't stop, which is remarkable," said Yoel Guzansky, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies.

This latest solo play is the third in Moran's trilogy, following The Tricky Part and All the Rage .
October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .

articles.title_orig: Fed Minutes Show Hawkish Unity Behind September Rate Hike
articles.title_zh: Fed Minutes Show Hawkish Unity Behind September Rate Hike
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.
"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated.
"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate."
The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years . And at the time, most Federal Open Market Committee members saw a need for at least one more 25 basis point rate hike this year.
Markets were banking on a hike and expecting more to come.
But economic data released in the past few weeks has changed the picture considerably. "Core" PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose a relatively cool 3% in August , beating expectations for a rise of 3.3% and marking a drop from 3.3% in July. Meanwhile, September jobs numbers fell far short of economists' expectations, with a gain of just 29,000 jobs , while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
That less rosy jobs picture, combined with a more positive read on inflation, had analysts — and some Fed officials — throwing cold water on the notion of another rate hike this month.
"This data won't shift the broader decision-making calculus for the Fed as inflation remains the supreme concern," Chris Hodge, chief economist for Natixis, previously told Yahoo Finance. "But with wages lower and the jobs picture a bit less rosy, it certainly decreases the urgency to hike in October (and perhaps December if inflation data cooperates)."
Even before the September job report, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams had already begun to temper expectations for a rate hike later this month . Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but that the central bank should take time to assess whether it's on a downward path.
Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."
The FOMC meets again Oct. 27-28. Futures markets see only a 17% chance of a rate hike this month, but a roughly 70% chance in December.

articles.title_orig: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.title_zh: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.content_orig:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has defended the police response, after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
In an address to the nation on Wednesday evening, he denied security forces had "orders to confront" the young people.
He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details.
The "anger of young people does not come from nowhere," he said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades - weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate.
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion".
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.
Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.
And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework.
Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.
Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented.
Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups".
"We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests.
Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage.
The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students".
The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April.
Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police".
The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day.
But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far.
The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."
