articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

articles.title_orig: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.title_zh: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.content_orig:
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years.
MINNEAPOLIS -- FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the AK-47 he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, the complaint says, agents sold him the gun and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent.
According to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, “yes i am 100% sure,” the complaint said, and added: “I would have backed out by now if I wasn't sure.”
The agent wrote that Mohamud's messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to fight in Somalia, ultimately for the Islamic State group. He later decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) is investigating reports of a second possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia after the death of a laboratory worker who was allegedly exposed to the illness.
Global health officials are pushing Moscow for transparency following the death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov.
Shipilova was admitted to hospital late last month with acute respiratory failure and placed on a ventilator before passing away on 2 October.
Local media reported that she was exposed to a dangerous pathogen after accidentally shattering a sample tube during routine laboratory work.
But senior Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov cast doubt on that account in comments to The Moscow Times earlier this week, pointing out that personnel at the institute operate in full protective suits.
"It's laughable," Favorov said. "If you break a test tube, the likelihood of infection is actually very low. In short, it doesn't matter to the general public – they'll believe the 'broken test tube' story."
"It's absolutely hair-raising," he added. "We will not be told what really happened."
Independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikal reported that a second individual with symptoms of severe pulmonary distress had died at an Irkutsk regional medical facility. The report has not been independently verified.
At least 197 people identified as direct or indirect contacts of the laboratory staff remain under medical isolation, with around 100 currently being monitored in hospital wards.
WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed that the UN agency has requested additional information from Russian health authorities regarding a second employee presenting with unexplained pneumonia.
In a statement released late on Tuesday, Dr Ghebreyesus pushed for Russia to release all known information about the outbreak: “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
But so far, official statements have appeared contradictory .
While municipal authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk posted a warning on Telegram urging residents to avoid traveling to Shelekhov, the message was removed from the official channel two hours later, according to Lyudi Baikal .
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighbouring Republic of Buryatia, also initially shared on social media that the technician had died of plague, before editing his post to state she "may have" been infected.
The conflicting official accounts have heightened concerns surrounding the disease. Regional outlets report that Shipilova worked with the bacterium Yersinia pestis – the same behind the “ Black Death ” that wiped out more than a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.
Moscow has informed the WHO that an epidemiological investigation has been completed and claims that testing has detected no high-threat pathogens among monitored contacts.
Unlike bubonic plague, which is transmitted through flea bites, pneumonic plague infects the lungs directly and can spread rapidly between humans via airborne respiratory droplets.
The WHO has stated that it remains in close contact with Russian authorities and has offered technical support to manage and contain any potential outbreak.

articles.title_orig: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.title_zh: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz has hit out at what he called political “extremism” in Germany after recent stinging defeats in local elections to far-right and far-left parties.
“This is a task for ⁠our society as ⁠a whole, and it is ⁠one I intend ⁠to play ⁠my part in,” he said on Wednesday at an ‌event in Berlin.
Merz said “extremism” was forcefully making its way into the country’s parliaments, a day after a member of the far-right Alternative for ‌Germany (AfD) was elected president of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt and the Left Party won out in Berlin’s state election last month.
“Anyone who casts their vote for ⁠the AfD is ⁠playing the extremists’ game and undermining credibility,” ⁠Merz said. “In ⁠any case, this is incompatible with the values of ‌my party, the CDU [Christian Democratic Union of Germany].”
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority it had had sought. AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch won the presidency of the parliament in the eastern German state Tuesday, backed by the left-populists in a secret ballot.
Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after about a million people fled to Germany in 2015, many of them from war-torn Syria.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with mainstream parties, though most traditional parties have pledged not to enter coalitions with the AfD.
Merz’s comments followed the far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on September 20, in another defeat for the chancellor’s ruling Christian Democrats.
Lead ‌candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through with a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party, which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980, said the increasingly difficult rental situation was the biggest social problem in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations she said drove property speculation, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 percent of voters backed a proposal to promulgate the move.
While the AfD has attracted most attention, the ⁠Left Party has also benefitted from a general turn against the mainstream centre-left and centre-right parties.
Meanwhile, Merz has received a record low approval rating . Earlier this month, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his performance, the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
Another major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters are set to elect a new parliament in April.

HUNTSVILLE, Ala. ( WAFF ) - A rare piece of World War II history is in Huntsville today. The B-29 Superfortress known as Doc is at Huntsville’s airport as part of a tour stop this week.
Doc is one of only two B-29s still flying today. More than 1,600 were built in Wichita during the war.
It is joined by a P-51 Mustang. Those are rare too. Only about 150 of them are still around.
Visitors got a chance to see the aircraft up close and learn about the crews who designed, built and flew them.
“It’s a pretty special opportunity...really makes the history jump off the page,” Josh Wells said.
Wells said the event also helps younger generations understand an important piece of history.

It follows the hobbit Frodo as he embarks on a quest—alongside a fellowship composed of an elf, a dwarf, some men, and other hobbits—to destroy the One Ring and save Middle Earth.
The Lord of the Rings stage musical first premiered in 2006 at Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto, before opening in the West End in 2007 at Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. A well-received production, which originated in 2023 at the Watermill Theatre in the U.K. just finished a North American and international tour. articles.title_zh: Asia Focus: Expanding Global Reach, World's Most Populous Continent Continues To Flourish
articles.content_orig:
Get Pollstar News and more delivered right to your inbox with Pollstar Daily Pulse.
By signing up, you agree to Pollstar’s Privacy Policy and Terms of Use
The Asian touring market continues to thrive, with promoters and venues reaping the rewards of artists both homegrown and international presenting top-notch concert productions at home and abroad, with new partnerships and long-lasting relationships behind the scenes meaning the traffic is both inbound as well as exported to the rest of the world.
The dominance of K-pop in the region, anchored by activity in Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Indonesia and Dubai, continues. The top four touring acts, as reported to Pollstar (see page 162), were K-pop bands, with SEVENTEEN showing the way with a gross of $97,394,005. TWICE grossed $76,176,781 and TOMORROW X TOGETHER did $53,035,381. Ranked No. 4, Korean powerhouse BTS grossed $49,069,994 in Asia as part of its mammoth “ARIRANG” world tour, which was No. 1 on Pollstar ’s Q3 chart. Those shows were the chart-topping boy band’s first in nearly four years due to military service.
Western acts were busy as well, with Lady Gaga leading the charge ($44,379,794 grossed), fifth overall in the territory, and Travis Scott was close behind ($37,922,441). Just to reinforce the Asian presence in the home region, G.E.M. came in seventh ($31,725,779), BLACKPINK is eighth ($29,193,966 grossed) and ENHYPEN nabbed the ninth spot ($21,562,532 grossed).
The key players in the region who Pollstar talked to were uniformly enthusiastic about business. HYBE was the leading promoter in the region with $247,965,087 in gross revenue. HYBE 360 President Yoojin Oh (Impact Honoree, see page 176), who oversees the company’s concert business, says, “Over the past year, HYBE artists’ global tours have continued to expand not only in scale but also in the breadth of markets they reach.”
Japan’s presence as the longtime leader in the Asian music industry remained strong. Three of the top five promotion agencies were Japanese and the country held six of the top 10 spots. The biggest player in the nation was Creativeman Productions, with $103,665,840 in gross revenue, third overall in Pollstar ’s Asia chart. Naoki Shimizu, president of the promoter behind the long-running Summer Sonic festival, notes, “The live music market has bounced back from the pandemic and is expanding even more than before.” Of Japan in particular, he says, “The breadth of the entertainment landscape is a key factor. There is a capacity to turn anything — whether local acts, Asian artists, Western music, anime, or voice actors — into a major live concert market.” In second place for promoters was Live Nation with $209,803,871 in gross revenue reported.
Dennis Argenzia, president of global touring, Asia-Pacific at Live Nation, has observed a shift in enthusiasm from artists. “Asia is at a really exciting point in its evolution as a live music market,” Argenzia says. “For many years, we had to convince artists and their teams to come to Asia — today, the conversation is very different. Artists want to perform here because they see the growth in demand and the opportunity to build deeper connections with fans across the region.”
Hong Kong appears as a microcosm of the expanding Asia market. The 50,000- capacity Kai Tak Stadium is a crucial venue for all of Asia. Kath Wong, senior manager at the firm that runs the stadium, emphasizes the outsized role K-pop plays in Asia touring and Hong Kong’s place in the market, with concert highlights from BLACKPINK and SEVENTEEN at Kai Tak Stadium.
“Each show serves as a milestone not only for Kai Tak Sports Park, but for Hong Kong as a whole,” Wong says. “It demonstrated that the stadium could host some of the world’s biggest touring artists and deliver complex international production to the standard expected by the artist, promoter and production teams.”
She expands on the environment, with Kai Tak Sports Park including both the 50,000-seat stadium with a retractable roof and the indoor Kai Tak Arena, which can accommodate 10,000 people and has 80% retractable seating.
Irene Chan, CEO of AsiaWorld-Expo, which operates the 14,000-cap arena of the same name in Hong Kong (the third biggest in Asia), is extremely upbeat on the business in 2026: “Audiences increasingly seek destination events that combine music, culture, fashion, art, retail, food and technology—driving the global trend of ‘festivalisation’ and creating new revenue and partnership opportunities beyond ticket sales.”
Global promoter AEG Presents, based in the U.S., is also focused on the region. Adam Wilkes, president and CEO of AEG Presents Europe and Asia-Pacific, who has worked in the Asian touring market for decades, offers a comprehensive overview.
“Asia is already a core part of the global touring ecosystem, and its significance will only grow,” he says. “International artists are reaching more markets, supported by a wave of world-class venues – both newly opened and under construction. The regional touring industry is also becoming more sophisticated, allowing artists to build meaningful careers across multiple countries rather than only at home.”
He adds that the world environment has changed, catapulting Asia to a new position. “Crucially, the traffic now moves both ways,” he says. “K-pop led the way, but Japanese, Chinese and Indian artists are increasingly finding audiences and performing at the highest level around the world. More inbound touring, better infrastructure and a growing pipeline of internationally successful Asian talent make the potential enormous.”
In Japan, Shimizu reflects on Creativeman’s successes but also looks forward.
“After Summer Sonic, the biggest tour of the year for us would be Iron Maiden,” he says of the globally renowned heavy metal pioneers. Other rock bands continue to show strength in the market. “Last year, it was Green Day, and Radiohead is coming up next year. It is a joy, after such a long career, to have tours every year by bands I’ve promoted for over two decades.”
The company is set to expand its dominant network even further. Shimizu explains, “Creativeman recently entered into a strategic partnership with AEG. In the past, artists like Taylor Swift, Justin Bieber and Ariana Grande have started out working with Creativeman for their Japan shows, only to move on to global tours handled by others. Now, however, we have a setting where we can continue working with them throughout that process. Furthermore, Creativeman’s 36 year-career will undoubtedly bring added value to AEG.”
Kaori Hayashi, president of Live Nation H.I.P. (Hayashi International Promotions), notes the promoter is set for a banner year. “We are seeing strong demand for live entertainment in Japan. More artists are touring, more live events are taking place, and more fans are attending these events. Bruno Mars’ 12-show dome tour in January 2027 will be the largest tour ever undertaken by an international artist in Japan. It will span six cities across the country – from Osaka to Nagoya – reflecting the depth of demand for international artists well beyond Tokyo, and is another indication of the scale of opportunity in this market.”
The 37,000-cap GMO Arena Saitama (formerly Saitama Super Arena), one of Japan’s biggest arenas and the second largest in Asia, has been closed for a major renovation since January. Operations will resume in April 2027, and Yutaka Minagawa, MD of the arena, tells Pollstar they have already secured a number of major international artist performances.
“Japan’s music market continues to benefit from strong and stable demand for domestic artists, particularly within the J-Pop genre,” Minagawa says. “In addition to J-Pop, K-Pop enjoys enduring popularity, while major international artists continue to include Japan as part of their world tours. This creates a highly diverse live entertainment ecosystem where multiple genres can successfully coexist.”

articles.title_zh: Paxton admits Trump’s Iran war and US gas prices are plaguing Republicans in leaked audio
articles.content_orig:
Texas attorney general acknowledged affordability was his party’s ‘biggest problem’ heading into the midterms
US politics live – latest updates
Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted privately that rising fuel prices as a result of Donald Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms in the latest leaked audio recording.
Asked what issues were “dragging” his campaign at a closed-door fundraising event, Paxton replied, “It’s not tariffs … it’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” according to an audio recording shared with Axios.
“When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch,” Paxton said.
Paxton acknowledged affordability was Republicans’ “biggest problem” heading into next month’s election, citing polling numbers that indicate Democrats are ahead in many competitive races – including his own.
Trump has tried to change the narrative around affordability, insisting his administration has done more to lower everyday prices for Americans than Democrats. Trump, who picked Paxton to run as the Republican in the Texas Senate race, will join Paxton at a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday evening.
But Paxton appeared to recognize the uphill battle facing Republicans , telling people at the closed-door events that “so many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable”.
“I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t, you know, I don’t know what’s behind some of the decisions,” Paxton said.
The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment.
Madison Cercy, a spokesperson for Paxton’s campaign, said in a statement that the Texas attorney general’s comments were “a non-story”.
“The attorneygeneral said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” Cercy said.
“President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families’ pockets with a bigger child tax credit and larger deductions for health care and buying a home. Texans need immediate relief, and everyone knows James Talarico will raise your taxes,” Cercy added.
Recent polling from the Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research indicates most adults blame Trump for poor economic conditions. Approximately 74% of Americans said the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs.
In the audio recording, obtained by Axios, Paxton said he was trying to help lower costs in ways that he could, such as through his proposed tax cut plan that includes healthcare and housing write-offs.
after newsletter promotion
Axios’s reporting is just the latest leaked audio clip of Paxton being critical of his own party.
Earlier this week, Politico reported that Paxton privately admitted to people at a closed-door event that outside forces in Washington DC were controlling much of his campaign messaging.
“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from DC,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico.
Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican midterm convention “dropped” his polling numbers.
Paxton is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico . Polls show Paxton and Talarico are neck-and-neck, but Talarico has a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

Nissan U.K.’s business unit will bring autonomous driving services to the university city of Cambridge and test its latest technology in an urban enviorment and create a blueprint to launch in other communities.
The plans are part of a government-funded research project backed by Nissan that launched in September 2023 at the University of Warwick with the goal of deploying an autonomous mobility service across the U.K.
The pilot trial, dubbed “ADventure,” will be coordinated between the automaker, local authorities, commuters and residents, the company said in its Sept. 28 release .
Using a specially adapted 2022 Nissan Leaf electric vehicle , the project hopes to focus on how future AD technology “can create social value, improve accessibility and address local transport challenges,” Nissan said.
The automaker used the common example of elderly people in the U.K. having to travel to a medical appointment when they do not drive themselves.
Nissan will draw on more than a decade of research by its engineers at the Nissan Technical Center Europe, which will lead the autonomous mobility project.
By choosing the driving environment in Cambridge for the automaker’s first real-world trial, Nissan aims to create a blueprint that it can refine and replicate across the U.K.
“This project is an important step for autonomous mobility in the UK,” said David Moss, SVP research and development for Nissan vehicles across the Africa, Middle East, India, Europe and Oceania regions. “With UK Government backing, it will take autonomous vehicle research beyond central London and into another city, helping us understand how these services can work for different communities and real-life journeys.”
“By developing and applying Nissan’s in-house expertise, combined with the wider knowledge from our partners, we can delve further into how self-driving vehicles can improve connectivity, accessibility and quality of everyday life,” Moss added.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.content_orig:
Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.
The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
after newsletter promotion
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall , this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.title_orig: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.title_zh: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.content_orig:
Lincoln University students and alumni filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the state of Missouri on Wednesday, alleging decades of unequal funding between it and the University of Missouri.
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri and is the first case brought by the 1890 Project challenging a state allegedly failing to appropriately fund an 1890 land-grant university, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers.
The 1890 Project monitors promises made in the federal government's second Morrill Act in 1890, which aimed to ensure historically Black universities were equitably funded as certain white universities had been through the original 1862 Morrill Act.
Lincoln students and alumni, as well as their lawyers, spoke on the lawsuit at a press conference Wednesday at the Missouri State Capitol Rotunda.
Lincoln students and alumni's attorney, Donald Callaway, explained that the Second Morrill Act of 1890 requires the state of Missouri to match the Federal research and extension dollars that come to Lincoln every year.
"From fiscal year 2000 through 2007, the state appropriated nothing towards that match, zero," Callaway said. "While it matched the University of Missouri in full and without condition."
These land-grant institutions were supposed to be provided funding for programs to strengthen research, extension and teaching, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture .
The New York Times reported that between 1987 and 2020 , federal officials found Missouri appropriated $361.6 million less to Lincoln on a per-student basis than to the University of Missouri.
The students and alumni are seeking a court-ordered remedy to combat the alleged disparity and permanently require that Missouri fully match Lincoln's federal land-grant funding.
They also allege that the funding disparity stems from the University of Missouri being founded in 1839 for white students and Lincoln University being separately designated as a land-grant institution in 1890 for Black students.

The University of Missouri is an 1862 land-grant university , established under different legislation than the 1890 land-grant universities.
The 1890 Project wrote that in Sept. 2023, the U.S. secretaries of agriculture and education documented more than $12 billion in funding shortfalls across 16 states.
These were measured between 1987 and 2020 and compared to each state's 1862 land-grant university.
The lawsuit's defendants include the Coordinating Board for Higher Education, Gov. Mike Kehoe, Commissioner of Higher Education and Workforce Development Bennett Boggs, and UM System President Mun Choi.

articles.title_orig: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.title_zh: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump has increasingly touted his drug pricing deals, claiming the U.S. is now paying the world’s lowest prescription drug prices. “This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” he recently said at the White House.
TrumpRx.gov, the public face of his drug pricing discounts, has grown dramatically since its launch in February. What started as a few dozen brand-name drugs now includes a catalog of more than 800 brand-name and generic medications, offering discounts on everything from popular weight loss drugs to treatments for cancer and rheumatoid arthritis.
It’s unclear whether the average American has “ saved a fortune,” as Trump promised .
Prescription drug prices fell by 3.1% over the year ending in July, according to federal inflation data — though experts say it’s too soon to know how much of the drop, if any, can be attributed to Trump’s drug pricing deals. The site has relied on GoodRx’s pricing data and technology to power many of its listings and blends pre-existing discounts from drugmakers with newly negotiated prices.
At the Republican midterm convention last month , Trump said, “We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world.”
A recent analysis from KFF finds that TrumpRx prices are competitive with prices in other countries for a small number of cancer and cholesterol medications. In many cases, Americans aren’t getting the best deals compared with the rest of the world.
Take Ozempic. For the average patient in the U.S. paying out of pocket, the blockbuster diabetes drug can cost $349 to more than $1,000 a month. It’s $349 through TrumpRx. Yet in several other wealthy countries, the next-highest price is $190 a month, according to KFF, a nonpartisan research group.
Enbrel is an even starker example. A monthly supply of the rheumatoid arthritis drug costs $3,354 through TrumpRx, more than five times the $641 average in the other countries where researchers found prices.
Some drugs, however, come out well ahead. Rydapt, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers, costs $2,909 for 56 capsules through TrumpRx — less than half the $5,901 price for the same amount in France, the next-cheapest country.
Those disparities run throughout the site, according to the KFF analysis. The report, which didn’t compare TrumpRx savings within the U.S., offers one of the first broad worldwide comparisons of Trump’s drug pricing claims.
The analysis looked at 32 brand-name drugs sold through TrumpRx that lacked generic or biosimilar equivalents. Researchers focused on those drugs because patients don’t have the option of switching to cheaper versions, meaning the discounts offered through TrumpRx could have a greater impact on what they pay.
The group compared the prices with those in 11 other wealthy countries, including Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The prices are current as of Aug. 26.
The results were almost evenly split. For 17 of the drugs, the TrumpRx prices were lower than the average prices abroad. For 15, they were higher. But Trump has promised Americans the lowest prices in the world. By that measure, the results were less favorable: Only five were actually the lowest-priced, while 13 were the highest-priced.
“It’s kind of a mixed bag,” said Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of the Medicare policy program at KFF, who co-authored the report. “Even with the reductions that may have been agreed to by manufacturers who are listing their drugs on the TrumpRx website, the prices that they’re offering, even at a discount, still continue to be higher than prices in comparable countries.”
The findings offer an early look at both the promise and the limits of Trump’s approach to lowering drug prices.
Americans routinely pay more for prescription drugs than patients in other wealthy countries, even when the medications are made by the same companies. The TrumpRx discounts, the White House says, stem from Trump’s “ most favored nation ” pricing deals, agreements with drugmakers to charge Americans the lower prices they offer other countries in exchange for tariff relief. But the discounts can vary widely, the analysis found, and they haven’t consistently produced the lowest prices Trump promised.
“I’m not surprised by these findings,” said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a primary care physician and health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School. “Any of us who have been following drug prices realized, as soon as TrumpRx was launched, it was a limited number of drugs and it was clear that the prices that were there were not always going to be linked or in any way related to what the prices are in other countries.”
It’s a markedly different approach from the one taken by Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden.
Rather than use Medicare’s power to negotiate prices for a limited number of costly drugs each year, TrumpRx relies largely on voluntary agreements with individual drugmakers to offer discounted prices directly to consumers. (The exact details of the agreements remain largely confidential, and the White House has declined to disclose them.)
TrumpRx doesn’t sell the drugs directly. For many drugs, it sends consumers to manufacturer programs through which they can obtain coupons or discounted cash prices without insurance.
That’s not how most people get their prescription drugs. About 9 in 10 Americans have some form of health insurance , meaning many pay for medications through private insurance, Medicare or Medicaid — although discounted cash-pay options have become increasingly popular as insurance has gotten more expensive. The money spent on TrumpRx doesn’t count toward a patient’s copay or deductible.
“They’re highly selected products where the manufacturer is willing to offer a discount,” Rome said. “Maybe they’re not the products causing the highest spending in the U.S. in some cases or are products where they were already offering confidential discounts, but now they’re making those discounts more public.”
The site now includes several cheaper, generic medications. “But those generics and the low prices for those generics pre-existed the TrumpRx website ,” Cubanski said.
The KFF analysis doesn’t capture every drug available through TrumpRx, and there are limits to how much can be concluded from it.
Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a group that tracks drug pricing in the U.S., counts about 80 brand-name drugs currently on TrumpRx, while KFF was able to compare prices for 32.
Part of the challenge, Ciaccia said, is that some drugs sold in the U.S. aren’t available in all of the countries KFF examined. That can make direct comparisons difficult.
“One of the big differences is the U.S. market does have more products in it than international markets, so that is noteworthy to the extent we have options here in the U.S. rather than a one-size-fits-all treatment approach,” he said.
International prices aren’t always perfectly comparable, either, he said. The analysis relied on publicly available prices, which may not include confidential discounts negotiated between foreign governments and drugmakers.
Ciaccia also noted that KFF’s 11 comparison countries don’t exactly match the countries used in some of the administration’s international pricing programs.
A White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for comment. The CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Those limitations don’t change the basic comparison at the heart of Trump’s claim: whether the prices offered to Americans match or beat those available abroad.
“We wanted to put that claim to the test with this analysis,” Cubanski said. “There is not a clear pattern across the board for higher prices or no consistent pattern across the board for lower prices. ”

Nova Music Festival survivor Natalie Sanandaji and Holocaust survivor Sami Steigmann join ‘America’s Newsroom’ on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks. Sanandaji recounts her fight for survival, while Steigmann warns about rising antisemitism around the world.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations blasted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his message marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks, comparing the mayor’s framing of the massacre to "turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists."
Ambassador Danny Danon accused Mamdani of trying to "hijack" the anniversary after the mayor commemorated the more than 1,100 Israelis killed by Hamas before pivoting to accusations of "genocide," "occupation" and "apartheid" against Israel .
"‘Mamdani-ism’ — an attempt to hijack the anniversary of October 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel," Danon wrote on X in response to the mayor’s post.

Israel's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Danny Danon, condemned New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani for using a message on the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attack to make accusations against Israel. (Reuters/David Dee Delgado)
"It is like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists," he added. "We will not let this happen. We will remember those who were murdered, and we will never forget who was behind this massacre."
Mamdani’s post Wednesday began by calling the anniversary "profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers" and describing the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack as "horrific war crimes."
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani smiles in reaction to reporters' comments after a private meeting with President Donald Trump at Gracie Mansion on Manhattan's Upper East Side, New York, N.Y., Sept. 21, 2026. (Anthony Behar/Sipa USA)
"On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others," Mamdani wrote. "We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."
DANNY DANON: FROM OCT 7 TO FLIGHT 1073: THE RESILIENCE THAT KEEPS ISRAEL STANDING
The mayor then turned much of his statement toward the war in Gaza, accusing the Israeli government of carrying out a "devastating, ongoing genocide" and citing a Palestinian death toll of more than 74,000, including more than 21,000 children.
"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," Mamdani wrote.
Mamdani accused Israel of bombing ambulances, targeting residential buildings and journalists with drone strikes and turning away food aid at border crossings. Israel has disputed allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, aid workers and journalists and has rejected accusations of genocide , noting flyers that the Israeli military has sent to Palestinian civilians warning them of attacks in advance and urging them to get to safety.
The mayor also accused the U.S. government of complicity in Israeli "war crimes" through its military support.

"Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment," Mamdani wrote. "To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity."
MAMDANI FIRES BACK AT NETANYAHU, CALLS ISRAELI LEADER 'ARCHITECT OF HORRIFIC GENOCIDE' AHEAD OF UN VISIT

"Disgusting and shameful to use October 7th as an excuse to repeat Hamas’ talking points. The terrorist enemies that seek to destroy us will not prevail. We stand with the Jewish people and we pray for the victims, their families and the survivors," said Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
"Shame on you for trying to blow a kiss and slap Israelis in the face at the same time," posted former U.S. Ambassador to the UN Nikki Haley. "On October 7, Hamas raped, burned, and murdered Israelis and Americans in front of their loved ones. They kidnapped others and tortured them for months. This is antisemitism, no matter how you try to put a bow on it. Israelis have every right to defend themselves. If this happened in the U.S., you can bet we would defend ourselves too."
". @NYCMayor , not once do you say 'Jews.' On Oct. 7, Hamas-led attackers murdered civilians, committed sexual violence, mutilated bodies and took hostages," said Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt. "You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points. The city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel deserves a mayor who can honor the dead without exploiting them."

articles.title_zh: 5 takeaways from Kemi Badenoch’s fighty Tory conference speech
articles.content_orig:
BIRMINGHAM, England — Kemi Badenoch used her rare moment in the spotlight Wednesday to promise “a fight coming in British politics; a fight that we have not seen in this country for more than half a century.”
Britain’s opposition Conservative leader, speaking at the close of her party’s annual conference in Birmingham, started as she meant to go on. She attacked Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour Party and her right-wing rivals, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
It was a speech more about positioning the Tories in a five-party system than about policy. What little she did announce was also about positioning.
Badenoch’s flagship pledge was to abolish inheritance tax on a person’s main home, which is currently set at a threshold of £500,000 (or £1 million for a married couple). It will overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest families — but it’s part of Badenoch’s argument about being unashamedly Tory and pursuing growth.
On her own terms, and those of her members, Badenoch is seeing the conference as a success. This time last year her own party was muttering about her future; now it is united in pursuing a victory at the next general election.
Whether she can achieve that victory is another question. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the Conservative Party on just 18% in a general election (due by 2029), beneath its historic low in 2024, and behind Reform on 22% and Labour on 26%.
POLITICO crunched the five biggest takeaways as Tory conference closed.
With most polls projecting a hung parliament, the shape of Britain’s next government could be decided by one thing: whether the Tories are willing — or able — to form a pact with the rival right-wing party Reform UK.
Badenoch’s speech suggests that they are neither — and made it personal. Badenoch, the first Black leader of a major U.K. political party, took aim at Reform politicians and outriders who have questioned if non-white Brits with foreign heritage can be classed as English.
“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are … I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country.”
She added: “To those who say unite the right: We are not uniting with that.”
At the same time, her party is clearly turning its head to middle-class “shire Tories” in the south of England who switched to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Some of the key policies announced this week — such as state-subsidized childcare for workers earning more than £100,000 a year, and scrapping inheritance tax on multi-million-pound family homes — will benefit wealthier voters in London and the south.
That is a very different voter coalition to the industrial heartlands in northern England, where low-income voters have turned to Reform. “None of our voters would benefit from this tax cut for the 2%,” boasted one Reform aide of the Tory inheritance tax policy. “They’ve abandoned going after our voters.” (Tory aides insist they have policies to win back both groups.)
So could Badenoch’s Conservatives form a pact with any other party? The jury’s out on that.
She spent little energy criticizing the hard-right Restore Britain – which could aid her party by splitting Reform’s vote – but Restore’s tally of seats at an election would be minimal.
And while the Tories governed with the centrist Liberal Democrats in 2010, both sides remain scarred from that. Meanwhile, Burnham has already laid out what sounded like a coalition pitch last week, when he argued for closer ties with the EU and electoral reform. Shadow Minister for Policy Renewal Neil O’Brien told a fringe event: “Not since Marilyn Monroe stood on that hot air vent and let her skirts billow have I seen such a ‘come hither’ gesture.”
Badenoch’s speech focused overwhelmingly on attacking her rivals and creating clear space between her party and theirs.
Burnham was the “Paddington Bear prime minister who hopes our problems go away”; Tory defector Robert Jenrick was part of an “export boom of drama queens going to Reform”; the Green Party was guilty of “disgraceful antisemitism”; some Reform politicians are “measuring up the curtains for their prison cells.” Her autocue even instructed her to give “side eye” when mocking Farage’s ally George Cottrell, whose links to the Reform leader have come under scrutiny.
It was a deliberate contrast to Burnham’s speech last week, which avoided naming his rivals. In a five- or six-party market, the two leaders are taking opposite approaches to make themselves stand out: Burnham wants to rise above the melee while Badenoch thew the hardest punches.
They are united, though, in seeing politics as a battle of ideas — unlike former PM Keir Starmer, accused of focusing more on process than vision. Badenoch spent more than two months personally writing a 95-page treatise on her ideas about the future, “The Right Way.” She unveiled it on the conference’s first day; extraordinarily, it didn’t leak.
Badenoch also wants to cut through by presenting her party as the voice of fiscal responsibility and defense. The Tories announced what they said would amount to £13 billion a year in welfare cuts on top of £23 billion announced last year. “Our country is running out of money. Almost every other problem flows from this,” said Badenoch.
She added her party would end the “delays” and approve a third runway for Heathrow Airport (though the exact process for this was not clear), halve the 15 percent rate of employers’ national insurance for under-25s and overturn the Labour government’s reforms to employment rights.
The Conservatives are banking on Burnham’s star falling after the Oct. 28 budget and a difficult spending review next year, in which he will have to set out whether Britain spends 3% of its GDP on defense by 2030.
A shadow cabinet minister, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said: “It’s a make-do-and-mend budget; they’ll get through that — but they can’t get through the spending review. [Former Chancellor] Rachel [Reeves] left them a bomb primed to explode.”
The ideological chasm being opened up between Badenoch and Burnham is forcing the Conservatives onto uncomfortable territory.
Burnham used his own conference speech to open the door to a possible return to the EU, but Badenoch was clear she didn’t want to take the bait.
“He [Burnham] wants to reopen the Brexit debate. Can you imagine having to go through that again?” the Tory leader said. “So much time lost arguing with ourselves, arguing with the EU, going round and round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again. I think that is a terrible idea.”
Public opinion has shifted in the decade since the EU referendum, which was triggered and implemented by the Conservatives. Renegotiating any new deal with Brussels will be a headache for Burnham and stacked with peril, but it’ll also serve as a reminder of what the Tories — and veteran Brexit campaigner Farage — delivered for the country.
Veteran Euroskeptic MP Bernard Jenkin was even blunter at a fringe event: “Do not defend Brexit. Brexit is toxic with the voters.”
The other big divide that Burnham opened up is on social care. He wants to fund a “national care service” for the elderly in part by changing the “triple lock” on state pensions.
That lock is cherished by many on the right — but there are also the small-state realists who want it axed to curtail the ballooning welfare bill. POLITICO reported that shadow cabinet ministers are debating not coming up with their own substantive offer on how to fix the care system.
“The Tories are ducking the big issues facing our country and instead of showing leadership, Kemi Badenoch is happy to fail a whole generation of older people who have contributed to society all their lives,” Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson responded.

articles.title_orig: Astronaut Christina Koch’s Eagles weekend was out of this world
articles.title_zh: Astronaut Christina Koch’s Eagles weekend was out of this world
articles.content_orig:
It's no secret that Eagles fans are a dedicated fanbase. However, only one can say that they have watched the team from space.
The Eagles celebrated Astronaut Christina Koch at Lincoln Financial Field as the Eagles' Honorary Captain during Sunday's game against the Rams. Known for circumnavigating the moon earlier this year with the Artemis II mission and crew, Koch also holds the world record for the longest time spent on the International Space Station in one deployment, with 328 straight days.
Even while orbiting 250 miles above the Earth's surface on the International Space Station, Koch would tune in for Eagles games.
"We have the ability to have an internet connection for personal things, crew choice things they call it. It's just a way to have things that can keep you entertained on the weekends and things that you love and remind you of home," Koch said. "I did marry into it. My husband (Robert) is a diehard, long-term Eagles fan since he was a kid. I resisted a little while mainly because I didn't know a lot about football ... now I'm all in and I've been sort of addicted ever since.
"If I didn't have time to watch them because they were at a different time where I couldn't make it, I would watch the reruns on the NFL Network or something like that. And it was just such a treat when I could share that with my husband and other people on Earth. It was a way of connecting through that and to just kick back and have a little bit of fun."
Astronaut (and Eagles fan) Christina Koch received a hero's welcome as an Honorary Captain against the Rams. After Sunday's game, the Artemis II crew member spent time with Eagles rookies, as well as science students from the Franklin Institute on Monday.

While Koch had been to Eagles games in-person before, she had never been to a home game at Lincoln Financial Field until Sunday. Not only did she join the Eagles Captains for the coin toss, Koch also led nearly 70,000 fans in an E-A-G-L-E-S chant during the two-minute warning of the first half. The woman who â quite literally â had ventured out into where no human has been before, said she was scared to start the Eagles' fight song.
"It was amazing to be at this place I've heard so much about, a place I looked at from space where I knew that all these fans came together with how dedicated they are," Koch said. "Just to be surrounded by that energy, to be right next to the players on the field, to watch their focus, watch them practice, watch their preparation rituals, it was amazing. I'm completely honored to have that opportunity."
Of course, Koch herself is no stranger to performing under pressure. During her time at the International Space Station, she participated in the first-ever all-female spacewalk, watching continents fly by below her feet as the station traveled at 17,500 miles an hour. For the Artemis II mission, Koch and the other astronauts trained for nearly three years, preparing for every single scenario â everything that could go wrong.
Koch's visit to the Eagles organization was part of NASA's Inspiration Tour, following the success of the Artemis II mission where Koch and the rest of the crew orbited farther from earth than any humans before. As it turns out, one of the many inspired by Artemis II was an Eagles Cheerleader. Before Sunday's game, Megan McKeon, a second-year cheerleader, had the opportunity to tell Koch that the mission inspired her to pursue a master's degree in planetary sciences.
"That moment was probably one of the most memorable and amazing ones of the whole game because she took the time to share her story personally with me and I could tell how much it meant to her and it truly did make an actual difference in her life," Koch said.
"I've been hearing stories like that from a lot of different people, but to meet someone firsthand that could tell me that they took the inspiration that the mission gave them and did something with it was really amazing. That was really all we ever wanted as a crew, was for it to have a positive impact on people's lives."
Koch also met Saquon Barkley on Saturday while touring the Jefferson Health Training Complex. The All-Pro running back had heard Koch was in the Eagles facility and set out to find her.
"He was super into space and the mission," Koch said.
The day after the game, the record-breaking astronaut spent time with Eagles rookies, as well as science students from the Franklin Institute on Monday. After being part of the Eagles' gameday experience, Koch got to show the Eagles rookies a glimpse into her world, answering questions before exploring the exhibits at the institute.
"Truth be told, that team inspires me, how they come into the arena and do their jobs under all that enormous, enormous pressure," Koch said. "It's been a source of inspiration. So, to be able to see it firsthand was really special." - Written by Caroline Connor

articles.title_orig: Cornell students plan seven-hour sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell students plan seven-hour sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University students began a seven-hour sit-in Wednesday in solidarity with Jane Doe, the woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity nearly two years ago.
“Seven hours for the seven hours she endured. Seven hours of solidarity. Seven hours demanding change,” a coalition of Cornell student groups said in a post on Instagram ahead of the demonstration.
Roughly 80 students had gathered inside a campus dining hall named for Pulitzer Prize-winning author Toni Morrison by around 3 p.m. Outside the building, students displayed posters bearing slogans such as “Justice for Jane Doe” and “Stop Protecting Rapists.”
The organizers said the sit-in is part of “Zero Day,” an “economic blackout calling on students to disrupt business as usual by not attending class or spending on campus.”
The protest illustrates the tense mood on the Ivy League campus following Jane Doe’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members last month, leading to renewed national attention on sexual misconduct and collegiate Greek life.
Three of the accused men have publicly denied the allegations through attorneys.
The sit-in comes two days after Cornell faculty members introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration over its handling of the alleged assault at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday night, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
Cornell has drawn intense scrutiny over how it responded to Jane Doe’s allegations in November 2024, and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has been criticized for declining to charge the accused. The university and the district attorney have each defended their original 2024 probes.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively replaced Van Houten as lead investigator last week, appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case. Cornell and Van Houten have publicly welcomed James’ involvement. “I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law,” Van Houten said in a statement on Friday.
Wednesday’s sit-in was announced on Instagram by a group of campus organizations, including Black Students United, Cornell NAACP, Mecha de Cornell, Planned Parenthood Generation Action at Cornell, Students for a Democratic Cornell, and a student-run chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union.
“The sit-in will be a space for students to share their support for survivors of sexual violence in myriad ways, including the share of resources and teach-ins,” the student groups said on Instagram.
Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.

articles.title_orig: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.title_zh: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.content_orig:
The first-ever international guidelines on managing childhood obesity from the World Health Organization (WHO) are raising the profile of GLP-1 treatments for kids and teens — but with strict criteria and a high degree of caution.
The new global guidance, released on Wednesday , recommends a broad range of interventions to manage diet, boost physical activity and change behaviours for the rising number of global youth living with obesity. And in certain cases, for some older children and teenagers, that could also mean medication or bariatric surgery.
The WHO doesn't recommend medical treatment, surgery or weight-loss devices for children up to the age of nine, the organization notes.
For older youth from the age of 10 to 19, medical treatments may be considered only when a supervised lifestyle program hasn't achieved results, the guidance states, while bariatric surgery should only be an option under strict conditions for youth living with severe obesity.
"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," said Dr. Luz María De Regil, the WHO's director of the department of nutrition and food safety.
Cheaper GLP-1s arrive in Canada: Are they safe?
London, Ont.-based pediatric endocrinologist Dr. Marina Ybarra welcomed the organization's cautious acknowledgement of medications as one avenue to tackle obesity.
Here in Canada, two GLP-1s are approved for weight management for youth aged 12 and up, but young patients typically have to pay for the drugs through their parents' insurance or out of pocket, said Ybarra, who works with Western University and leads the London Health Sciences Centre Children's Hospital pediatric weight management clinic.
Obesity Canada launches partnership aimed at improving care in health system
"The news about WHO encouraging GLP-1 as a possible treatment for children living with obesity — I think it's very good news," she said.
"Because maybe that will help us to get funding through the public system in Canada for children living with obesity. That's my biggest hope."
The WHO's new guidance is meant to tackle skyrocketing rates of obesity among global youth.
Roughly 170 million children and teens around the world between the ages of five to 19 were living with obesity in 2024, the WHO noted. Obesity prevalence in this age group has also quadrupled since 1990, rising from two to eight per cent.
The global recommendations echo recent Canadian guidance to manage obesity in children. That long-awaited 2025 update also called for behavioural and psychological support and, in some cases, additional medical or surgical interventions.
How family doctors navigate the rise of weight loss drugs
Can GLP-1s curb more than your desire for food?
But Canadian physicians recommend only using GLP-1s to manage obesity in children after the age of 12, two years above the WHO's cutoff due, and don't stipulate that medical intervention should only be tried after lifestyle changes.
" There is no evidence to support a stepwise approach whereby pharmacologic and surgical interventions should be offered only if behavioural and psychological interventions prove ineffective," reads the guidance published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.
"Using shared decision-making with families, health care providers should consider all intervention options."
The WHO, in contrast, focused on the "practicality and universality" of diet, physical activity and behavioural changes as the pillars of obesity management, and it stressed the need for "structured long-term follow-up" in cases where patients use medication alongside other lifestyle interventions.
Weight comes back quickly after quitting GLP-1 drugs: study
GLP-1s and other similar medications — known by household brand names like Ozempic, Mounjaro, Rybelsus, Wegovy and Zepbound — have exploded in popularity among adults to treat obesity and diabetes, and for general weight loss, even without a clear medical need .
The drugs work by mimicking the body's glucagon-like peptide-1 hormone, which helps manage appetite, slow digestion and regulate blood sugar.
Ybarra stressed the medications are now an effective tool for many young patients with obesity, helping to both reduce weight and improve quality of life.
1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada
While some children and teens face similar side effects to older patients, including nausea and other gastrointestinal issues, "we didn't see many of the severe complications that were seen in the adult population," Ybarra noted.
Younger and younger patients are also trying this growing class of drugs.
One U.S. study, published in the medical journal Pediatrics in September , revealed a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for children ages eight to 11, shooting up from 0.03 per cent to more than nine per cent between 2019 and 2026 — though overall use in this younger group remains rare.
Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits
Still, the WHO stressed the need for caution regarding GLP-1 use among children and teens, given limited research and the potential for misuse among certain groups, such as athletes or patients with eating disorders.
The WHO's new guidelines note that overall evidence linked to various medication treatments for childhood obesity, including GLP-1s and other drugs such as metformin or sibutramine, was "generally of low quality due to short term follow-up and evaluation, and [due to] the small numbers of studies and participants."
Ybarra agreed there's a lack of long-term data for the use of GLP-1s among youth, given how new these drugs are for younger patients.
"The data we have though, it's very reassuring and helpful — in terms of there's more benefits than risks."
GLP-1s and cancer prevention: What’s known and what isn’t
As for the line in the sand regarding children under 10 avoiding GLP-1s, the WHO's María De Regil stressed in a Tuesday news conference that the agency "recommends prioritizing other interventions in this age group."
"However, it is clear that the research is going in this area," she said. "Some national pediatric associations may recommend it."
Serena Williams’ return to tennis sparks conversation about GLP-1 drugs in sports
Denmark's Novo Nordisk and U.S.-based Eli Lilly are among the drug makers currently trialling pediatric obesity medications for kids as young as six, though María De Regil wouldn’t speculate on how any of those ongoing trials might change the WHO's recommendations.
Major questions still remain about how children should safely use these types of drugs, and for how long, stressed María De Regil.
"We realize that this is a rapidly evolving field," she said.

articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. We hope to share our award-winning experiences with you soon.”
The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
This year, Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes for the annual awards, determining the very best in hotels, resorts, spas, airlines, and more worldwide. The results will be featured in the magazine’s November issue.
Kristi Palma is the travel writer for Boston.com, focusing on the six New England states. She covers airlines, hotels, and things to do across Boston and New England. She is the author of the award-winning Scenic Six , a weekly travel newsletter.

Amazon announced its first smart lock that eliminates the need for a physical backup key should its rechargeable battery die while you’re away from home. While other smart locks lean on hidden USB ports or metal contacts for connecting a 9-volt battery to replenish a dead battery, the new Ring Smart Lock incorporates a more convenient charger right into its thumb-turn dial. Amazon doesn’t specify how many turns are needed but claims just “a few times” can generate enough power to unlock the door so you can gain access to your home and fully recharge the lock’s battery.
The Ring Smart Lock is expected to be available in the US sometime in early 2027 (pending FCC approval) and will be offered in black, silver, and brass finishes for $249. Unlocking options include a fingerprint reader and a backlit touchscreen keypad with the option to register multiple users and schedule when they have access to your home. This includes setting up temporary access codes that automatically expire after a set amount of time. The Ring Smart Lock can also be opened, locked, and monitored using the Ring mobile app or controlled using voice commands through Alexa-compatible devices like Echo smart speakers.
Installation doesn’t require any wiring since the Smart Lock uses Ring’s replaceable Quick Release Ultra Battery Pack , and instead of relying on your home’s Wi-Fi, the lock wirelessly connects to other devices using Amazon’s low-power, low-bandwidth, long-range Sidewalk network . Assuming you live somewhere with adequate Sidewalk coverage, you won’t have to worry about Wi-Fi outages preventing you from granting remote access or getting alerts about who’s just entered your home.
The Ring Smart Lock doesn’t include a camera, so you’ll need to pair it with a smart doorbell to see who’s accessing your home or one of five new Ring security cameras expanding Amazon’s collection of “Retinal Vision 4K” devices that first debuted a year ago. Starting today, you can preorder the new $149.99 Outdoor Cam 4K Plus that’s available in battery, wired, solar, and PoE versions, the $199.99 Spotlight Cam 4K Plus featuring a 550-lumen deterrent light, and the $219.99 Floodlight Cam 4K Plus that can illuminate large spaces while offering 24/7 recording with smart subject detection. But you won’t have to wait for the first indoor Ring camera with Retinal 4K. The $99.99 Indoor Cam 4K is available for purchase today and features a 115-degree field of view with a shutter that physically blocks the camera when privacy is needed.
Alongside all the new 4K options, Amazon is also introducing a new entry-level 2K indoor camera that’s available starting today for $69.99 . The Ring Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K uses “computer vision–based motion detection” to track subjects like pets moving around a room. The camera can rotate a full 360 degrees while tilting 175 degrees to keep subjects in frame, and like Ring’s new 4K indoor camera, the 2K version incorporates a physical privacy shutter that disables both the camera and its microphone when it’s closed.
